title: Being Recorded
description: Being recorded is different from being watched: the camera is impassive, the image will persist, and someone else is controlling what gets captured. Each of those differences carries its own quality.
equipment: A phone or camera. Storage that you both have access to and control of.
safetyNote: Agree before starting where the recording will be stored, who can access it, and whether it will be kept or deleted. Both people should have equal access to the storage. Do not record without explicit agreement from everyone in the frame.

instructions.label: Solo first
instructions.content: Record yourself alone — not to share, just to capture. Watch it back. Notice what seeing yourself from outside produces: whether it matches your internal experience of being in your own body, what surprises you, and whether the experience of watching yourself is primarily uncomfortable, neutral, or something that produces a positive response. You're separating your response to being captured from your response to being seen by someone else.

instructions.label: With a partner
instructions.content: One partner holds the camera; the other is the subject. The person recording controls the frame — what gets included, what doesn't, from which angle. The subject's job is to notice what being specifically framed and captured — rather than just generally observed — produces. After ten to fifteen minutes, swap. Both people get the experience of controlling the frame and of being in it.

explore: Solo: does watching yourself back produce recognition, surprise, or something harder to place — does it match what you expected to see?
As the person being recorded: does knowing what's being captured — being specifically framed — change how you're in the experience?
As the person recording: does controlling the frame — choosing what to include and exclude — produce any engagement of its own?
Does the knowledge that the recording persists change anything about the experience while it's being made?
why: Being recorded differs from being watched in a specific way: the camera is impassive and the image will exist after the moment ends. The person recording is choosing the frame — deciding what gets captured and from what angle — which is a particular kind of attention that live observation doesn't replicate. For the subject, being specifically framed often produces a quality of self-consciousness or heightened presence that general observation doesn't, because the frame makes the capture precise. The persistence of the recording is also its own variable: many people find that knowing something exists beyond the moment changes how they're in it, for better or worse.
